opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
Here is the full verse:

“Come now, let us set things right, says the LORD:
Though your sins be like scarlet, they may become white as snow;
Though they be crimson red, they may become white as wool.”

A few things are happening in this sentence that are easy to miss.

First, the phrase “Come now” is an invitation. God is not withdrawing from a sinful people. He is calling them into conversation.

Second, “let us set things right” (many translations say “let us reason together”) is courtroom language. God is essentially saying:
Bring your case. Let’s examine this honestly.

Not because He needs information.
Because He wants repentance to become understanding, not just fear.

Third, the imagery:
	Scarlet / crimson – ancient dyes that stain permanently. Once fabric was dyed this color, it could not be washed out.
	Yet God says He can reverse what humans cannot.

So the structure of the verse is powerful: Invitation – Come. Honest reckoning – Let’s examine the truth. Radical mercy – Even what looks permanent can be cleansed.

It is not sentimental forgiveness. It is transformational cleansing.

Isaiah begins his book by accusing Israel of corruption, injustice, and hollow religion. Yet right in the middle of that indictment, God says:

“Come. Let’s deal with this.”

That is the heart of biblical repentance:
not hiding from God, but walking toward Him with the truth of what we are.
